summary: No orders: futures point to a strong bounce this morning after the worst week since April 2025, but one good morning is not the buy-back signal the plan sets, so the cash waits for that signal or 10 December at the latest, and the health care fund stays because it is still above its sell line.
thesis:
Where the account stands. At the end of Friday 20 November it was worth $966.82 against $907.87 for the benchmark, $1,000 left in an S&P 500 fund. The gap grew to about $59 on Friday, almost all of it because the account was 85% cash on a day the S&P 500 fell 3.7%. Eight trading days is still far too short to call that skill; it came from rules written before the fall, not from predicting it.

What has happened since the last decision:

- Friday was a seventh straight down day and the worst of the week. The S&P 500 fell 3.7%, the Nasdaq about 5.3% and the Dow about 1.9%. Chip makers took the worst of it: the semiconductor fund SMH fell 10.6%, Nvidia and Arm about 14% each. The S&P 500 and the Dow ended more than 10% below their record highs. Worries about whether spending on artificial intelligence will pay off came on top of Fed Governor Waller's call for a half-point rate increase in December, and new US limits on chip exports.
- The places I would expect to hold up did: consumer staples (XLP) rose 0.7%, health care (XLV) slipped only 0.1%, and the bond funds rose about 1%. The 10-year Treasury yield fell to about 4.91% from above 5%.
- This morning, before the open, futures point to the S&P 500 about 2.2% to 2.9% higher and the Nasdaq 100 about 2.8% to 3.6% higher. Strategists at several banks called last week's fall a buying opportunity, Nvidia is up about 7% before the open, and Oracle said funding for its AI contract with OpenAI is secured. Others warn the selling may not be over. US crude is near $82. There were attacks on ships near the Strait of Hormuz over the weekend, but oil fell anyway.
- This is a short week. October PCE inflation, the Fed's preferred measure, comes out on Wednesday and is expected around 3.8% over a year, the highest in three years. Markets are closed on Thursday for Thanksgiving and close early on Friday. The Fed decides on 9 December.

Each holding judged against what I wrote when I bought it:

1. XLV: keep. It ended Friday at $177.24. The line is a close below $176, or a widening of the Medicare proposal to cut payments for drug makers or hospitals. Neither has happened: it is 0.7% above $176 and 0.4% above its 50-day average ($176.50), and I found no change to the Medicare proposal. On Friday it did what a defensive holding should, falling 0.1% while the market fell 3.7%. It is about 7% below what I paid, near the 8% loss limit (about $175). I would not add to it at this price. If it ends any day below $176, the next decision sells it.

2. Cash, about $827 (85%). The plan says SPY is bought back when it ends two trading days in a row at least 1% above its 200-day average, which is $732.76; that means two closes above about $740. SPY ended Friday at $689.81, about 6% below its 200-day average. Even a 3% rise today would leave it near $710, still well short. A sharp bounce after seven down days is common and often does not last, and the plan was written precisely so the account does not chase one good morning and pay fees to step in and out. So I wait.

I am clear that this is a large bet against a fully invested benchmark. Its end date stands as written: the account goes back to being fully invested no later than the first trading day after the Fed decision of 9 December, that is 10 December, whether or not the signal comes. If the bounce holds and SPY reaches the signal first, the cash goes in then.

I looked at three other uses for the cash. Consumer staples (XLP) has held up and sits above its 50 and 200-day averages, but holding it for about 12 trading days would cost about 0.3% in fees, and on a rebound day it would likely lag the market, so the gain over cash is not clear enough. A Treasury bill fund (SGOV) pays about the same as its fees for a stay this short. Longer bond funds (IEF, TLT) have risen as yields fell, but a hot PCE reading on Wednesday or a half-point Fed increase could reverse that. None of these has a specific, checkable reason today, which the plan requires.

This is not the first decision of the month, so there is no monthly review. The first is due at the start of December.
risks: The biggest risk is missing a rebound: with 85% in cash, every day the market rises the account gives back part of its lead over the benchmark, and if the rebound is fast the buy-back price could be higher than where SPY was sold. The opposite risk is that the 10 December date forces the account back in while the market is still falling. XLV is within about 1% of its sell line and could be sold soon at a loss. A hot inflation reading on Wednesday or a half-point Fed increase could hit everything the account might buy. Before-the-open futures can change by 9:30, the figures quoted differ somewhat between sources and were taken at different times, and one of the news pages could not be read.
